title.narrative: Enhanced Access Food Security and WASH Services for IDPs, Vulnerable Host Communities and Returnees in Aleppo and Hama Governorates

description.narrative: ltpgtOver the past decade, Syria has been overwhelmed by a series of compounded crises. Key drivers include Lebanon’s economic meltdown, unilateral sanctions, the COVID-19 pandemic, the 2023 earthquake, and ongoing conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza, and Lebanon. Additionally, in December 2024, changes in the administrative setup of Syria have further exacerbated the humanitarian crisis, especially with an increasing number of returnees and a lack of resources in the hosting communities. ltbrgtPopulation movements and renewed displacement continue across Syria. According to the latest data from the IDP Task Force (as of 19 May 2025), more than 1.14 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) have returned to their areas of origin since early December 2024. As of 22 May 2025, UNHCR estimates that 507,672 Syrians have returned from neighboring countries to Syria since 8 December 2024, bringing the total number of cross-border returnees to 868,512 since the beginning of 2024.nbsp ltbrgtFurthermore, around 1.5 million Syrian refugees are expected to return to Syria in 2025 (source: UNHCR).2According to the 2025 Humanitarian Response Priorities for Syria, it is estimated that approximately 16.5 million people, counting fornbsp more than 70% of the Syrian population, need humanitarian assistance.More than 14 million people are in need of WASH services, with 3.2 million individuals requiring WASH assistance in Aleppo, and overnbsp 420,000 individuals in Hama. Regarding Food Security, approximately 14.5 million people face food security challenges. Within this group, approximately 3.5 million reside in Aleppo, and around 780,000 in Hama, all requiring food and agricultural support.ltbrgtOperating under the organization's strategic pillars: Bread/Food Security and WASH. The proposed integrated response addresses the critical and interconnected needs of vulnerable IDPs, host communities, and returnees in areas severely affected by conflict, economic collapse, and the aftermath of the 2023 earthquake. ltbrgtHEKS/EPER's proposed activities fall under the SHF allocation strategy by providing sustained, multi-sectoral assistance in food security and WASH. Specifically: ltbrgtUnder envelope 1: To improve access to affordable staple food, HEKS/EPER will support access to subsidized bread production through: ltbrgt Rehabilitation of the Atareb Bakery building, including installation of a new generator to ensure consistent operation. (After rehabilitation works are completed, HEKS/EPER will fund the installation of a new production line.) ltbrgt Installation of a newl production line in Midan Bakery in Aleppo to meet the increasing demand of the growing population. Since HEKS/EPER previously rehabilitated the Midan Bakery, no additional building rehabilitation works are required.nbsp ltbrgtUnder envelope 2: To enhance access to clean water and mitigate public health risks in crisis-affected communities, HEKS/EPER will implement: ltbrgt Rehabilitation of two water pumping stations in Aleppo (Hur and Sahara) and two water pumping stations in Hama (Lower Amiqa and Hasraya). The Sahara pumping station will be solarized to ensure a sustainable and cost-effective energy supply. Since Hur couldn't be rehabilitated, the latter was replaced by Mkelbis pumping Station.ltbrgtBy targeting severely affected areas with high concentrations of IDPs, returnees, and vulnerable host populations, the intervention directly contributes to the overall allocation strategy objectives. The proposed response reinforces HEKS/EPER’s commitment to locally driven, context-adapted, and sustainable humanitarian programming in Syria's most affected areas. ltbrgtlt/pgt
